# Prompt

> `/ropensci-skills:run-complexity`

(Invoked with no arguments, against the working tree at `fix/table1-custodian-sort`,
commit `6cb96e0`, clean.)

# Skill

`ropensci-skills:run-complexity` v1.0.0, from
`~/.claude/plugins/cache/ropensci-skills/ropensci-skills/1.0.0/skills/run-complexity`.
Its operative instructions:

> **Measure first.** Rank functions by a real metric before reading source; the
> eye is a poor complexity meter and misses structural duplication entirely.
>
> **Read the code to interpret the numbers.** A high score can be benign (a chain
> of `&&` guards); a low score can hide 85× duplication. The metric points; you
> judge.
>
> **Confirm behavioural claims with runtime probes.** If you say a function is
> inert or its error path is broken, reproduce it in a scratch session and paste
> the result.
>
> **Read-only.** No refactoring the package to prove a point.
>
> **Preserve the user-facing surface.** Every internal-refactor recommendation
> must keep exported names, signatures, and return types identical.

Report skeleton: the shared template at
`run-package-review/references/report-template.md`.

**One documented deviation from the skill's method.** Step 1 prescribes
`devtools::load_all()` and measurement over a package namespace. `midwifery` has
no `DESCRIPTION` and is not a package — it is a pipeline of numbered scripts, by
design — so there is no namespace to load and no exported surface. Functions were
therefore read from source instead: each tracked `.R` file is parsed, and every
top-level `name <- function(...)` assignment is evaluated in a fresh environment
(a closure's body does not run at definition time) and the resulting closure
measured. This reaches **more** than `load_all()` would, since it covers
script-local functions that never enter a namespace; it reaches **less** in one
respect, noted under *Not run*.

# Report

## Method

Reproducible. Four scripts, all in
`/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-tylermuffly-midwifery/c7970797-eb02-408a-a4c2-bd39f8250800/scratchpad/`:

| script | what it did |
|---|---|
| `cc_measure.R` | cyclomatic complexity, LOC, max brace-nesting depth, `if`/loop counts, arity for every top-level function in every tracked non-test `.R` file → `cc.csv` |
| `dup_measure.R` | exact body-duplication groups (normalised deparse, grouped); call-site counts for every repo-defined helper via `utils::getParseData()` over `SYMBOL_FUNCTION_CALL` tokens |
| `own_cc.R` | re-measured the top 12 with every nested `function(...)` replaced by `NULL`, to separate a function's **own** branching from complexity it merely **houses** |
| `catalog_dup.R` | enumerated and body-hashed the nested closures inside the single largest offender |

Runtime probes (`probe_norm.R`, `probe_rck.R`, `probe_rck2.R`, `probe_na.R`)
confirmed each behavioural claim below; their output is pasted inline where
cited.

Versions: R 4.5.2 (`aarch64-apple-darwin20`), cyclocomp 1.1.2, stringr 1.6.0,
dplyr 1.2.1.

Scope: 959 top-level function definitions across 279 tracked `.R` files.
`tests/`, `@archive/` and `scratch/` excluded.

**No repository files were modified.** `git status` was clean before and after;
every probe ran in `/private/tmp/.../scratchpad` or sourced repo files read-only
into a throwaway session.

## Headline

**Amber, and the amber is concentrated — not diffuse.** Per-function complexity
across the pipeline is healthy: median cyclomatic complexity 2, mean 4.8, and 735
of 959 functions score 5 or below. Only 7 functions exceed 50, and two of those
turn out to be measurement artefacts rather than god-functions.

The real issues are the three the metric alone would not have told you:

1. `mw_build_catalog()` — 913 lines, **own** complexity 107, housing **30 nested
   closures** in one scope, in which the name `g` is bound **three times** and
   `pick` **three times**. Two of the three `g` bindings take the same arity and
   incompatible argument types, 41 lines apart, in the function that produces
   every number in the manuscript.
2. `R/join_safety.R` carries **four** near-parallel join wrappers, 595 deparsed
   lines, with 22 lines common to all four. The repo has already paid for this
   twice — *Bug 6* and *Bug 30*, both logged in the source, both "a guard
   `safe_left_join` had that `safe_inner_join` was missing." A **third** instance
   of the same drift is still open and confirmed by probe: `require_complete_keys`
   defaults to `TRUE`, is documented as a validation, and has **no effect on any
   reachable code path**.
3. One person-name normaliser exists **four times under four names** with
   divergent behaviour — and one of the four is **platform-dependent**, so the
   same midwife's name keys differently on the author's Mac than on a Linux CI
   runner. The repo's `H4` hygiene gate cannot see any of this, because it
   compares function *names*, and these four have four different names.

Caveat that matters most: finding 1 is a **latent hazard, not a live defect**. I
checked every current call site and all of them resolve to the binding their
author intended. The finding is that nothing stops the next edit from being
wrong, and nothing would catch it.

`cyclocomp()` scores a closure's entire body, nested closures included, so a
function that merely *houses* six helpers inherits all six scores. Reading
`cc_own` first stops two functions being accused of being god-functions when
they are modules with private parts.

### Hotspot 1 — `mw_build_catalog()`: one scope, 30 closures, three `g`s _(High.)_

`manuscript/R/build_stats_catalog.R`. 913 deparsed lines, 65 top-level
statements, own cyclomatic complexity 107, and 30 nested function definitions.
This is the only genuine god-function in the tree, and it is the one that matters
most, because it is the indirection layer that produces every number in the
manuscript — no figure in the paper is typed by hand, they all come out of here.

The structural problem is not the length. It is that 30 closures share one flat
913-line scope, and **two names are bound three times each**:

```
line  465:  g    <- function(e, s, col) { r <- pick(e, s); if (is.null(r)) NA_real_ else r[[col]] }
line  560:  g    <- function(r, col)    if (nrow(r)) r[[col]][1] else NA_real_
line  601:  g    <- function(k, col)    { r <- vs[vs$stratum == k, ]
                                          if (nrow(r)) r[[col]][1] else NA_real_ }

line  461:  pick <- function(e, s)                  { ... }
line  841:  pick <- function(rx)                    { ... }
line 1246:  pick <- function(frame, pattern, column){ ... }
```

The `pick` trio is comparatively safe: the arities differ (2 / 1 / 3), so calling
the wrong one errors loudly. **The `g` pair at 560 and 601 is not.** Both take
exactly two arguments. The first expects `r` to be a **data frame** and subsets
it directly; the second expects `k` to be a **character stratum key** and uses it
to subset the captured `vs`. They are 41 lines apart in one scope, and R gives no
warning when the second rebinding silently replaces the first.

I verified that **no current call site is wrong**: `g(r30, "diff_pp")` at 563–590
resolves to the 560 binding and passes a data frame, and `g("resolved_by_absence_c2",
"n_study_cohort")` at 606+ resolves to the 601 binding and passes a key. All
correct today. The hazard is that moving, copying or inserting one `mutate()`
across the line-601 boundary — the single most ordinary edit anyone makes in a
913-line builder — silently changes which function runs, in the code path that
decides what the paper claims.

There is a second, smaller instance of the same pattern:

```
line 1245:  num  <- function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
line 1466:  num_ <- function(v) as.numeric(v)
```

Two coercers for one job, 220 lines apart, differing in whether an unparseable
value fails loudly or becomes `NA` in silence. Which behaviour a statistic gets
depends on which spelling the author happened to type.

**Why the repo's own gates do not catch this.** `tests/ci_hygiene.R` H4 exists for
exactly this defect class, and its comment names the incident: "`norm_addr`
existed four times with divergent behaviour, `zip5` three." But H4 collects
definitions with `regexpr("^[.A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_.]*(?= *<- *function)")` —
anchored at `^`, so **top-level definitions only** (`tests/ci_hygiene.R:141`).
Thirty closures indented inside one function are invisible to it, including two
names bound three times each.

**Concrete fix, surface unchanged.** `mw_build_catalog()` is called from the
manuscript and from four tests; its name, arity and return value must not move.
Split the body at its existing section boundaries into file-level internal
builders — `.cat_linkage()`, `.cat_bands()`, `.cat_veto()`, … — each taking the
frames it needs and returning its own slice of the catalog, with
`mw_build_catalog()` reduced to sourcing its inputs and `c()`-ing the slices
together. Each accessor then lives in exactly one builder's scope, where a second
`g` is a visible redefinition in a 40-line function rather than an invisible one
in a 913-line function. Pick one spelling of the numeric coercer and delete the
other.

Smallest useful step if the split is too large for one commit: rename the three
`g`s and three `pick`s to say what they read (`g_link`, `g_row`, `g_stratum`).
That is a mechanical, reviewable diff that removes the whole hazard class without
restructuring anything.

**Gate that would hold it closed.** Extend H4 to collect nested definitions too,
and fail when one name is bound more than once **within a single function scope**.
That is a different and stricter law than H4's current cross-file one, and it is
the law that was actually broken here.

### Hotspot 2 — four parallel join wrappers, and a validation that never runs _(High.)_

`R/join_safety.R` defines four wrappers over `dplyr`:

| wrapper | line | LOC |
|---|---|---|
| `safe_left_join` | 618 | 251 |
| `safe_inner_join` | 1109 | 167 |
| `safe_semi_join` | 1494 | 90 |
| `safe_anti_join` | 1745 | 87 |

595 deparsed lines. Measured pairwise overlap, counting identical trimmed lines:

```
safe_left_join   vs safe_inner_join    65  (39% of the smaller)
safe_left_join   vs safe_semi_join     27  (30%)
safe_left_join   vs safe_anti_join     22  (25%)
safe_inner_join  vs safe_semi_join     30  (33%)
safe_inner_join  vs safe_anti_join     25  (29%)
safe_semi_join   vs safe_anti_join     43  (49%)

lines shared by ALL FOUR: 22
```

`safe_left_join` and `safe_inner_join` share 16 of their 17 and 16 parameters;
the signatures differ by three names only (`expect_unique_right` +
`require_complete_keys` on left, `expect_unique_both` on inner). Everything
else — key harmonisation, coverage reporting, duplication gating, the integrity
ledger, the report writer — is written out twice.

**This is not a hypothetical maintenance cost. The source records two bugs
already paid for it**, at `R/join_safety.R:1307` and `:1309`:

```r
# BUG FIX (2026-01-27): Bug 30 - Enforce max_duplication like safe_left_join
if (!is.null(max_duplication) && left_n > 0) {
  # Bug 6 fix: safe_left_join uses default=0; safe_inner_join was missing it.
```

Both are the same failure: a guard present in one wrapper, absent in its
near-twin, found later, fixed in the copy rather than at the root. Each fix left
the structure that produced it intact, so the next one is still available.

**A third instance is still open, and confirmed by probe.** `safe_left_join`
takes `require_complete_keys = TRUE` (`:624`), documents it in roxygen as a
validation, and reads it in exactly one other place — `:746`, inside the
`use_enhanced_metrics` branch:

```
$ grep -n require_complete_keys R/join_safety.R
624:                           require_complete_keys = TRUE,
746:      require_complete_keys = require_complete_keys,
```

That branch forwards to `safe_left_join_with_metrics()` from `R/join_metrics.R`
— **a file that does not exist in this repository**, which the code itself says
at `:629`: *"it requires `safe_left_join_with_metrics()` from `R/join_metrics.R`,
and that file does not exist in this repo."* `use_enhanced_metrics` was therefore
defaulted to `FALSE`, which is correct — and which makes
`require_complete_keys` unreachable on every path a caller can take.

Probe (`probe_rck2.R`), with `NA` in the join key on both sides so an incomplete
key is definitely present:

```
require_complete_keys = TRUE  -> "ERROR: Join coverage 66.7% below 98.0% threshold..."
require_complete_keys = FALSE -> "ERROR: Join coverage 66.7% below 98.0% threshold..."
identical results: TRUE
TRUE raised no condition about the incomplete key: FALSE
```

Identical. The flag changes nothing. The incomplete key is caught — but by the
coverage gate, which would have caught it with the flag set either way. A caller
who reads the docs and passes `require_complete_keys = TRUE` believes they have
switched on a check they have not. `safe_inner_join` does not offer the parameter
at all, which is the drift: one wrapper grew an option its twin never got, and
the option turned out to be inert in both.

**Concrete fix, surface unchanged.** Factor the shared body into one internal
`.safe_join_core(left, right, by, how = c("left", "inner", "semi", "anti"), ...)`
and make the four public names **explicit thin shims** — written out, not
generated by a factory, so `?safe_left_join`, autocomplete and
`@inheritParams` keep working, and so the diff stays reviewable:

```r
safe_left_join <- function(left, right, by, expect_unique_right = TRUE, ...) {
  .safe_join_core(left, right, by, how = "left",
                  expect_unique_right = expect_unique_right, ...)
}
```

Names, arities, defaults and return types stay byte-identical; `tests/test-join-safety.R`
and the other five suites that name these functions should pass untouched, which
is the check that the refactor was behaviour-preserving.

Then make one decision about `require_complete_keys`, and either way the lie
stops: implement the check in the core (one `anyNA()` over the `by` columns,
raising when `TRUE`), or delete the parameter and the roxygen that advertises it.
Implementing it is the better choice in a file whose entire purpose is to refuse
unsafe joins — but it is a **behaviour change** for existing callers that
currently rely on the default silently doing nothing, so it belongs in its own
commit with its own test, not folded into the deduplication.

### Hotspot 3 — one name normaliser, four spellings, one of them platform-dependent _(High.)_

Cyclomatic complexity is blind to this entirely: each of these functions scores
1–2. It surfaced from the duplication pass.

Outside `tests/`, the tree has only **7** exact body-duplication groups covering
14 definitions — genuinely clean. But **5 of the 7 are the same body under
different names**, which is the shape `H4` structurally cannot see, and two of
those five are in the one category H4's own comment singles out as the dangerous
one: *"never a JOIN KEY or a normalisation — the two categories where divergence
silently changes results."*

| name | file:line | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `audit2013_norm` | `audit_2013_dac_vs_nppes.R:187` | identical body to `drift_norm` |
| `drift_norm` | `build_identity_drift_prior.R:86` | identical body to `audit2013_norm` |
| `normalize_name` | `R/build_amcb_state_licenses.R:46` | same pipeline, different `NA` handling |
| *(inline)* | `amcb_license_bridge.R:111–121` | same pipeline **plus** `iconv(to = "ASCII//TRANSLIT")` |
| `dac_spine_collapse_set` | `build_dac_identity_spine_2013.R:186` | identical body to `drift_collapse_set` |
| `drift_collapse_set` | `build_identity_drift_prior.R:151` | identical body; builds a person-level set key |

These are not incidental. `drift_norm` feeds `first_2013` / `last_2013` /
`state_2013` and their `_2026` counterparts (`build_identity_drift_prior.R:134–179`);
`audit2013_norm` feeds `state_agrees = audit2013_norm(practice_state) ==
audit2013_norm(nppes_state)` (`audit_2013_dac_vs_nppes.R:214`); `normalize_name`
feeds `.block_surname_norm` (`expand_former_name_candidates.R:210`), a **blocking
key for candidate generation**. They *are* the comparison.

Probe (`probe_norm.R`), the four live spellings plus the repo's own `norm_org`
rule, on the two inputs that distinguish them:

```
     input drift_norm normalize_name    bridge org_rule
     Muñoz      MU OZ          MU OZ    MU NOZ    MU OZ
     Munoz      MUNOZ          MUNOZ     MUNOZ    MUNOZ
   O’Brien    O BRIEN        O BRIEN   O BRIEN   OBRIEN
    OBrien     OBRIEN         OBRIEN    OBRIEN   OBRIEN
 St Mary's  ST MARY S      ST MARY S ST MARY S ST MARYS
```

Three distinct consequences, all confirmed:

**(a) The bridge normaliser is platform-dependent.** Its `iconv()` step is
supposed to fold accents before `[^A-Z0-9 ]` strips them. On this machine it does
not:

```
locale: en_US.UTF-8
iconv TRANSLIT raw on this machine:  ‘Mu~noz’
platform: aarch64-apple-darwin20
```

macOS libiconv transliterates `ñ` to the two characters `~n`; the `~` is then
replaced by a space, giving `MU NOZ`. glibc's iconv on a Linux CI runner
transliterates the same character to a bare `n`, giving `MUNOZ`. I verified the
macOS half directly, above; the glibc half is the long-documented
libiconv-vs-glibc `//TRANSLIT` difference and I have not executed it here, so
treat that half as high-confidence but unexecuted. Either way the *mechanism* is
confirmed: the key this script produces depends on which machine ran it, in a
repo whose author works on a Mac and whose gates run on Linux.

**(b) Accented names fail to match their own unaccented spelling.** `Muñoz` and
`Munoz` are the same midwife recorded by two arms. All four normalisers key them
differently (`MU OZ` vs `MUNOZ`, or `MU NOZ` vs `MUNOZ`), so they land as a
disagreement rather than a match:

```
drift_norm  Munoz vs Muñoz : FALSE
bridge      Munoz vs Muñoz : FALSE
```

**(c) The repo already learned the apostrophe lesson and did not apply it here.**
`R/lib/org_names.R:28` carries the fix and its incident, in a comment:

> *"Apostrophes are DELETED, not turned into a space. Turning them into a space
> splits every possessive, so `ST MARY'S HOSPITAL` keyed as `ST MARY S HOSPITAL`
> and never matched `ST MARYS HOSPITAL` — two spellings of one organization,
> recorded differently by two arms, counted as a disagreement."*

All four person-name normalisers turn `'` into a space. The same incident is
therefore live for people — `O'Brien` keys as `O BRIEN` and never matches
`OBrien` — in a cohort of nurse-midwives, a population where apostrophised
surnames are common:

```
drift_norm  OBrien vs O’Brien: FALSE
org_rule    OBrien vs O’Brien: TRUE
```

`norm_org` also handles curly apostrophes, noting NPPES and Care Compare disagree
on which they use; none of the four person-name copies does.

**Concrete fix.** One `norm_person_name()` in `R/lib/`, beside `norm_org()` and
built on the same three decisions `norm_org` already paid for (delete
apostrophes including curly ones; fold accents with a deterministic explicit map,
**not** `iconv(//TRANSLIT)`, whose output varies by platform; then strip and
squish). Replace all four call sites with it. This is a **key-changing** fix — it
will move match counts, which is the point — so it needs the same treatment any
normalisation change gets here: run it as a shadow arm and compare arm to arm,
never shadow-vs-freeze.

**Gate that would hold it closed.** H4 compares names, so it cannot see a
renamed copy. The complement is a body-level law: hash each tracked top-level
function's normalised body and fail when two definitions in different files
share a hash, with an allowlist in the shape H4 already uses. `dup_measure.R`
from this review is most of that gate — it finds 7 groups today, so the baseline
starts at 7 and shrinks. Catching copies that were also *renamed* is exactly the
gap this hotspot came out of.

### Hotspot 4 — the two highest-own-complexity functions with no direct test _(Medium.)_

`county_sentences()` (`R/10-county-birth-profiles.R:125`) scores 82 with **no
nested closures** — all 82 is its own branching, from 35 `if` expressions across
104 lines. `district_sentences()` (`R/12-district-profiles.R:358`) scores 38 the
same way. They generate the prose that appears on the county and district
profiles: each `if` is a guard choosing a sentence form based on which values are
present, which is a legitimate shape for the job and not a defect.

The gap is coverage. Searching `tests/` for the names of the twelve hotspots:

| function | tests naming it |
|---|---|
| `mw_build_catalog` | 4 |
| `safe_left_join` | 6 |
| `safe_inner_join` | 4 |
| `validate_source_coverage` | 2 |
| `classify_apparent_move` | 1 |
| **`county_sentences`** | **0** |
| **`district_sentences`** | **0** |

Every other hotspot is pinned by at least one test. These two — the highest own
complexity in the repo after the catalog builder and the join wrappers — are
named by none. Each branch is a reader-facing claim about a county, and several
carry comments recording that the wording was already wrong once and corrected
(the ascertainment hedge at `:143–153`, the clause-stacking at `:161–163`). Those
are exactly the decisions a test should hold.

This is a test-coverage finding surfaced by a complexity pass, not a complexity
finding; `run-test-audit` is the right pass to size it properly. Flagging it here
because the ranking put it in front of me: complexity concentrated in untested
branches is where the next defect goes.

**Concrete fix.** Not a refactor — the nesting is shallow (depth 2) and the
branches are independent, so splitting buys little. One table-driven test:
a handful of synthetic `r` rows chosen to hit the documented branch boundaries
(`n_cnm_cm == 0`, `== 1`, `> 1`; `rucc_2023` absent, as it is for territories
and for counties added since the 2023 vintage; each `fmt()` returning `NULL`),
asserting the sentence each produces. That pins the wording decisions the
comments say were hard-won.

### Minor

**`duckdb_scan_for_raw_connections` is not a god-function** _(Low — no action.)_
`R/lib/medicare_duckdb.R:422`, cc 98, which ranks it second overall and is
misleading: `cc_own` is **3**. All 95 of the rest live in six named nested
closures (`callee_name`, `is_bare_duckdb_driver_call`, `is_bare_duckdb_driver_ref`,
`walk_calls`, `collect_driver_aliases`, …). It is a static analyser whose helpers
are scoped inside it, and each closure carries a comment explaining the evasion
it closes. Lifting the six to file-level internals would make each separately
testable and would drop the headline number; it would also widen their visibility
for no behavioural gain. Worth doing only if someone wants to unit-test the
walker directly. `.code_closure` (`R/lib/artifact_provenance.R:99`, cc 40,
`cc_own` 7) is the same artefact at smaller scale.

**`walk_calls` swallows every error at three levels** _(Low.)_
`R/lib/medicare_duckdb.R`, inside the scanner: a `tryCatch` wrapping a loop whose
body is itself `tryCatch(..., error = function(e) invisible(NULL))`. A node the
walker cannot descend into is skipped silently, so a malformed region of a file
being scanned reduces the gate's coverage without saying so. The function's own
comment argues this trade deliberately and bounds it ("an explicit, documented
'where practical' limit"), which is why this is Low and not a finding —
but counting the skips and reporting a non-zero count would turn a silent blind
spot into a visible one for one line of code.

**`pick` is bound 11 times across the repo** _(Low.)_ Eight top-level definitions
(`analysis/compare_linkage_arms.R:4`, `compare_nppes_to_dac_demographics.R:190`,
`enrich_amcb_crosswalk_geography.R:124`, `extract_archive_origins.R:36`,
`extract_dac_midwives.R:64`, `extract_nppes_subannual_panel.R:78`,
`link_practice_locations_to_org_npi.R:99`, `resolve_org_ambiguity.R:126`) with
eight different contracts — `pick(d)`, `pick(have, ..., what)`, `pick(...)`,
`pick(cands)`, `pick(pat)` — plus the three nested in `mw_build_catalog`. `pick`
is on H4's `ALLOW` list, and H4's stated line holds: none of these is a join key
or a normalisation, they are column- and file-choosers local to one script. No
action, but the allowlist entry is doing more work than its justification
("a genuinely private one-liner") describes, and it is worth knowing that `pick`
means eleven different things in this tree.

**`join_coverage_report()` is called positionally** _(Low.)_
`R/join_safety.R:832` and `:1305` both call it as
`join_coverage_report(left_n, matched_rows, label_left, label_right, min_coverage)`
against a signature declared at `:413` with more parameters. Positional calls
across a five-argument boundary in a function whose later parameters are
validation thresholds are how an inserted parameter silently shifts a threshold.
Naming the arguments is a one-line change per call site. It folds naturally into
the Hotspot 2 refactor, where both call sites collapse into one.

## Caller-facing recommendations (surface unchanged, but worth noting)

Not refactors — discoverability points, kept separate and **optional**:

- **`require_complete_keys` should not be documented as working** until it does.
  Whichever way Hotspot 2 resolves, the roxygen at `R/join_safety.R:560`–`:566`
  currently describes a validation a caller cannot switch on. Of everything in
  this report this is the item most likely to mislead someone reading the docs
  rather than the source.
- **`num` vs `num_` in the catalog builder** reads like a typo and is a semantic
  distinction (warnings suppressed or not). If both spellings survive the
  Hotspot 1 split, name them for what they do (`num_quiet` / `num_strict`).
- **The three `g`s and three `pick`s could be self-describing for free.** Even
  with no restructuring, `g_link` / `g_row` / `g_stratum` makes the next reader's
  job possible and the next editor's mistake visible.

## Verified healthy (no action)

- **The complexity distribution itself.** 76.6% of 959 functions score 5 or
  below; median 2. For a 654-file pipeline accreted over years, per-function
  complexity is genuinely under control. The problems in this report are seven
  functions, not a pervasive condition.
- **Duplication outside tests is minimal and real.** 7 exact-body groups covering
  14 of 959 definitions. The largest is 2 copies × 21 lines
  (`assign_county_from_points`, already on H4's allowlist with a reason). For a
  repo this size that is a low number, and it means Hotspot 3 is a specific
  problem rather than a symptom of general copy-paste.
- **`na_matches = "never"` is applied consistently.** My probe initially looked
  like a bug: three left rows in, two out, coverage 66.7%, and `dplyr::left_join`
  gives three rows for the same input because dplyr matches `NA` to `NA` by
  default. It is not a bug. `R/join_safety.R` passes `na_matches = "never"` to
  the join *and* to every accounting call that measures it — `:803` (the join),
  `:793` and `:764` (the anti-join accounting), `:932`, `:1295`, `:1304`,
  `:1552`, `:1801`. The policy (two records that both lack an identifier are not
  the same person) is the right one for identity linkage, it is the opposite of
  dplyr's default, and it is applied in all ten places rather than nine. That
  consistency is what made the apparent discrepancy resolvable in one grep.
- **The duplication that exists in `tests/` is deliberate and documented.** The
  `chk` / `ok` / `bad` / `skip` harness repeats across 49, 8, and more files, and
  H4's allowlist carries a paragraph justifying each as console plumbing, never a
  join key or a normalisation, with a dated note recording six entries *removed*
  in 2026-11-16 once they stopped repeating. An allowlist that shrinks is working.
- **The high-complexity functions are commented where it counts.** `county_sentences`,
  `duckdb_scan_for_raw_connections` and `classify_apparent_move` each explain
  *why* a branch exists, several citing the incident that created it. That is the
  difference between 82 branches you can review and 82 you cannot.

## Not run (reason)

- **No package-namespace measurement.** No `DESCRIPTION`, so no
  `devtools::load_all()` and no exported-surface analysis. Deviation documented
  under *Skill*.
- **Nested closures were not measured repo-wide.** `cc_measure.R` and
  `dup_measure.R` collect **top-level** definitions only, matching H4's
  convention. `mw_build_catalog`'s 30 closures were enumerated by hand
  (`catalog_dup.R`) *because* the profile pointed there. A repo-wide nested pass
  would likely find more of Hotspot 1's shape elsewhere, and is the obvious next
  measurement — it is also what the proposed gate would require.
- **`tests/` excluded from the complexity profile.** 249 of 654 tracked `.R`
  files. Test complexity is a different question, and `run-test-audit` owns it.
- **No pipeline execution.** Nothing in this review ran a pipeline step, read the
  frozen cohort, touched DuckDB, or hit a network or paid API. Every probe used
  three- to five-row synthetic frames. Consequently nothing here is a claim about
  runtime cost or memory — that is `run-performance-review`.
- **The glibc half of the `iconv` finding is unexecuted.** macOS libiconv's
  `Mu~noz` output is pasted above from this machine. The glibc comparison is
  stated from documented behaviour, not run. It does not affect the finding's
  substance: a key whose value depends on the C library is a problem whichever
  direction the difference runs.
- **No files modified**, per the skill's read-only rule. Every recommendation is
  a proposal.

## Suggested fix priority

1. **Rename the three `g`s and three `pick`s in `mw_build_catalog`** _(High,
   Hotspot 1.)_ Mechanical, no behaviour change, removes a live shadowing hazard
   in the code that produces every published number. Do this before the split,
   not after — it is the cheap half of the fix and it is independently valuable.
2. **Consolidate the four person-name normalisers into one `norm_person_name()`**
   _(High, Hotspot 3.)_ Highest consequence in the report: it changes match
   outcomes today, silently, differently on different machines. Build it on
   `norm_org`'s three paid-for decisions; replace `iconv(//TRANSLIT)` with an
   explicit map; validate shadow-arm against shadow-arm.
3. **Resolve `require_complete_keys`** _(High, Hotspot 2.)_ Implement it or delete
   it, in its own commit with its own test. A documented, defaulted-on validation
   that does nothing is worse than no validation in a file whose job is refusing
   unsafe joins.
4. **Factor the four join wrappers onto one core with explicit shims** _(Medium,
   Hotspot 2.)_ Bug 6 and Bug 30 are the same bug twice; the structure that
   produced them is still there. Larger diff than items 1–3, which is why it sits
   below them, but it is the one that stops the fourth instance.
5. **Split `mw_build_catalog` at its section boundaries** _(Medium, Hotspot 1.)_
   The real fix for a 913-line function with own complexity 107. Surface stays
   identical; the four tests naming it are the check.
6. **Add the nested-rebinding law to H4, and a body-hash law beside it** _(Medium,
   Hotspots 1 and 3.)_ Two gates for the two blind spots this review found in an
   existing gate: one name bound twice in one scope, and one body under two
   names. `dup_measure.R` is most of the second already.
7. **Table-driven test for `county_sentences` and `district_sentences`** _(Medium,
   Hotspot 4.)_ cc 82 and 38, no test naming either.
8. **Name the arguments at the two `join_coverage_report()` call sites** _(Low,
   Minor.)_ One line each; folds into item 4.
9. **Count and report `walk_calls`'s skipped nodes** _(Low, Minor.)_ One line;
   turns a documented blind spot into a visible one.
